description_full: Costco Wholesale Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the operation of membership warehouses in the United States, Puerto Rico, Canada, Mexico, Japan, the United Kingdom, Korea, Australia, Taiwan, China, Spain, France, Sweden, Iceland, and New Zealand. It offers merchandise, including sundries, dry groceries, candies, coolers, freezers, liquor, and tobacco; non-food merchandise comprising consumer electronics, appliances, small electrics, health and beauty aids, hardware, lawn and garden, sporting goods, tires, toys and seasonal, automotive, stamps, tickets, apparel, furniture, domestics, housewares, special order kiosks, and jewelry; and fresh food, such as meat, produce, deli, and bakery products. The company is also involved in warehouse ancillary operations, which include gasoline, pharmacies, food courts, optical, hearing aids, and tire installation centers. In addition, it engages in e-commerce, business centers, travel, and other businesses. Further, the company operates e-commerce sites; and offers branded and private-label products in various categories. The company was formerly known as Costco Companies, Inc. and changed its name to Costco Wholesale Corporation in August 1999. Costco Wholesale Corporation was founded in 1976 and is based in Issaquah, Washington.

financial_summary: Costco Wholesale Corporation is a mega-cap consumer defensive business with a $466.9B market cap on $303.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 41% against a 8% cost of capital — a 32-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $9.4B in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.71× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 81× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.7%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).

Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+8.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 20% and a beta of 0.75, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.12 vs 5y 0.72), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.9B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 14% in the 2020 crash, 31% in the 2022 bear market and 48% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $432 (margin of safety -144%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 12%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $346 to $550 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 50.7 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 32.5 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 49.8 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 51% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 37 covering analysts target $1,068 on average, 1% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 41% clears the cost of capital of 8.5% by 32pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.32).
It converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.71x.
ROE of 26% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $15.1B (3% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.8% over 3 years, 9.1% over 5 years and 9.8% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 58% of profits supports about 23.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs 2.4x depreciation (2.1% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 74%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $5.3M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.7% (0.2% in buybacks and 0.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 21 consecutive years, though it has been cut 15.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 355,000 employees, each generates about $854K of revenue, 1.7x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 8.9% a year.
